{{DISPLAYTITLE:Lake and Lean projects}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/A library of mathematics}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A single Lean source file can be checked with the command <code>lean</code>. Anything larger,
a library of hundreds of files or a program with dependencies, is organised as a '''Lake
package''' and compiled by '''Lake''', Lean's build tool, which ships with every version of
Lean. Which version of Lean a project uses is fixed by a one-line file and enforced by
'''elan''', the toolchain manager. This page shows a minimal project as files, the commands
that compile and test it, and how dependencies are pinned, all with Lean 4.34.1 and the Lake
that comes with it.

== The toolchain ==

A Lean '''toolchain''' is the set of programs and files for one version of Lean, among them
<code>lean</code> itself, <code>lake</code>, a C compiler (<code>leanc</code>, a version of Clang), the
program <code>leanchecker</code>, and the compiled standard library and runtime. Toolchains
are installed and selected by elan.<ref name="rm-bt">"Build Tools and Distribution", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/]</ref>
The <code>lean</code> and <code>lake</code> commands a user types are small proxies installed
by elan. Each looks for a file named <code>lean-toolchain</code> in the current directory and
its parents, reads the toolchain named there, installs it if it is missing, and runs the
program from that toolchain. A command can also name a toolchain directly, as in
<code>lake +leanprover/lean4:v4.34.1 new greeting</code>.<ref name="rm-elan">"Managing Toolchains with Elan", section 24.2 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/]</ref>

The file holds one line:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">leanprover/lean4:v4.34.1</pre>

The part before the colon names where toolchains come from, and the part after it the
version. A project's file should name an exact version, not a channel such as
<code>stable</code>, so that everyone working on it uses the same Lean. Changing the version
is a one-line edit; the new toolchain is downloaded the next time it is
needed.<ref name="rm-elan" /> This matters more for a proof assistant than for most
languages. The elaborator, the tactics and the library change from one version of Lean to
the next, and a proof that is accepted under one version may fail under another. The
toolchain file records under which version a body of proofs was checked.

== A minimal Lake package ==

<code>lake new greeting</code> creates a directory with a library, an executable and a
configuration file. With Lean 4.34.1 the configuration it writes, <code>lakefile.toml</code>,
is:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">name = "greeting"
version = "0.1.0"
defaultTargets = ["greeting"]

[[lean_lib]]
name = "Greeting"

[[lean_exe]]
name = "greeting"
root = "Main"</pre>

The first lines describe the Lake package itself. Each <code><nowiki>[[lean_lib]]</nowiki></code> table
declares a '''library''', a collection of Lean modules under a root name, here
<code>Greeting</code>; each <code><nowiki>[[lean_exe]]</nowiki></code> declares an '''executable''', a
program whose Lean module defines <code>main</code>.<ref name="rm-lake">"Lake", section 24.1 of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), including 24.1.1 "Concepts and Terminology", 24.1.1.2 "Builds", 24.1.1.5 "Test and Lint Drivers" and the TOML configuration reference. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/]</ref>
The source files follow the names. <code>Greeting.lean</code> is the root of the library and
imports its parts:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">-- This module serves as the root of the `Greeting` library.
-- Import modules here that should be built as part of the library.
import Greeting.Basic</pre>

<code>Greeting/Basic.lean</code> holds the one definition:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">def hello := "world"</pre>

and <code>Main.lean</code> is the program:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">import Greeting

def main : IO Unit :=
  IO.println s!"Hello, {hello}!"</pre>

A Lean module's name is its path: <code>Greeting/Basic.lean</code> is the Lean module
<code>Greeting.Basic</code>, and <code>import Greeting.Basic</code> refers to it. Lake reads
the imports to work out the order in which the Lean modules must be compiled.<ref name="rm-lake" />

The configuration can also be written in Lean, as <code>lakefile.lean</code>. <code>lake new
greet2 std.lean</code> writes:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">import Lake
open Lake DSL

package "greet2" where
  version := v!"0.1.0"

lean_lib «Greet2» where
  -- add library configuration options here

@[default_target]
lean_exe "greet2" where
  root := `Main</pre>

The TOML form is purely declarative. The Lean form is a Lean program and can compute its
configuration or define new kinds of target.<ref name="rm-lake" />

== Compiling ==

<code>lake build</code> compiles the default targets and everything they need. In the new
directory it reports:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">info: greeting: no previous manifest, creating one from scratch
info: toolchain not updated; already up-to-date
✔ [2/8] Built Greeting.Basic (277ms)
✔ [3/8] Built Greeting.Basic:c.o (58ms)
✔ [4/8] Built Greeting (225ms)
✔ [5/8] Built Greeting:c.o (66ms)
✔ [6/8] Built Main (244ms)
✔ [7/8] Built Main:c.o (69ms)
✔ [8/8] Built greeting:exe (289ms)
Build completed successfully (8 jobs).</pre>

The first two lines appear on the first run only, and the times in brackets vary from run
to run. Each Lean module is elaborated, which produces an <code>.olean</code> file holding
its definitions and theorems in compiled form, and C code, which is compiled to an object file (<code>:c.o</code>); the
object files are linked into the executable. <code>lake exe greeting</code> then prints
<code>Hello, world!</code>.

Elaboration includes the Lean kernel's check of every definition and theorem, so a
Lake build of a Lean module that finishes without errors or warnings gives the same assurance
as opening it in an editor and seeing it accepted: every theorem in it, and in everything it
imports, has been checked. The reference manual makes the comparison explicitly.<ref name="rm-validating">"Validating a Lean Proof", a chapter of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.34.0), section "The Blue Double Check Marks". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/]</ref>

Running <code>lake build</code> again with nothing changed prints only <code>Build completed
successfully (8 jobs).</code> Lake keeps a '''trace''' for every output, recording a digest of
each input from which it was made; when no input has changed, the output is reused and its
saved messages are replayed instead of being produced again.<ref name="rm-lake" /> Lake keeps its
working state under the directory <code>.lake/</code>: compiled outputs in
<code>.lake/build/</code> and the sources of dependencies in
<code>.lake/packages/</code>.<ref name="rm-lake" />

== Testing ==

<code>lake test</code> runs the Lake package's '''test driver''', a target named in the
configuration. Lake is not a test framework: it finds the driver, compiles it, and, for an
executable, runs it and treats a non-zero exit code as failure. A library can serve as the
driver, and then any elaboration error counts as a failure, including a failed
<code>#guard</code>.<ref name="rm-lake" /> Adding <code>testDriver = "GreetingTest"</code>
and a second library to the configuration,

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">[[lean_lib]]
name = "GreetingTest"</pre>

with the file <code>GreetingTest.lean</code>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">import Greeting

#guard hello == "world"
#guard hello.length == 5</pre>

makes <code>lake test</code> succeed. Changing the last line to claim a length of 6 makes it
fail, with this among its messages:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">error: GreetingTest.lean:4:0: Expression
  hello.length == 6
did not evaluate to `true`</pre>

For a library of proofs the distinction between compiling and testing is thin. A theorem
that is false, or whose proof is broken, does not compile.

== Dependencies ==

A Lake package may require others. In <code>lakefile.toml</code> each dependency is a
<code><nowiki>[[require]]</nowiki></code> table. A dependency can come from Reservoir, an online index of Lake
packages, from a Git repository at a given revision, or from a local
path.<ref name="rm-lake" /> The reference manual's example of a dependency taken from
Reservoir is:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">[[require]]
name = "example"
version = "≥2.12.0"
scope = "exampleDev"</pre>

The configuration says which dependencies are wanted. The file
<code>lake-manifest.json</code> says exactly which versions are in use: for each dependency
it records the source and the precise revision. Lake brings each dependency's local copy into
line with lake-manifest.json before compiling, and creates the file if it is missing;
<code>lake update</code> moves the recorded revisions forward. The file is meant to be kept
with the source.<ref name="rm-lake" /> For the minimal project, which has no dependencies,
Lake wrote:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">{"version": "1.2.0",
 "packagesDir": ".lake/packages",
 "packages": [],
 "name": "greeting",
 "lakeDir": ".lake",
 "fixedToolchain": false}</pre>

Together, <code>lean-toolchain</code>, the configuration file and lake-manifest.json fix the
version of Lean and the exact source of every dependency. That is what makes a Lean project
reproducible: another person, or the same person years later, can obtain the same toolchain
and the same dependencies and have every proof checked again. The large mathematical
libraries described in [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/A library of mathematics|a library
of mathematics]] are distributed in this form.
